title: Place of Supply (POS) Engine: Inter-State vs Intra-State Determinism

parts.title: Dual GST Constitutional Matrix: Section 7 & 8 IGST Act Inter-State vs Intra-State Tax
parts.say:
Welcome to Day 9 of Corporate Taxation & GST. Today, we master the geopolitical jurisdictional engine of the Goods and Services Tax: the 'Place of Supply' (POS). Because India operates a federal Dual GST model—where the Central Government and State Governments share concurrent taxation powers under Article 246A of the Constitution—every commercial invoice must be categorized as either an 'Intra-State Supply' or an 'Inter-State Supply'. Charging the wrong tax type is not a harmless clerical error; it leads to severe compliance friction, interest penalties, and cash flow strain.

The legal test for determining tax classification is governed by Section 7 and Section 8 of the Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) Act. Under Section 8, an 'Intra-State Supply' occurs when the 'Location of the Supplier' (LOS) and the 'Place of Supply' (POS) are in the SAME State or Union Territory. In this case, two concurrent taxes are charged: Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) (or UTGST). Under Section 7, an 'Inter-State Supply' occurs when the Location of Supplier and the Place of Supply are in DIFFERENT States, different Union Territories, or one is in a State and the other in a Union Territory. In this scenario, a single unified Integrated GST (IGST) is levied by the Centre and subsequently apportioned to the consuming destination state under Article 269A.

What happens if an enterprise makes a mistake—charging CGST+SGST on a transaction that tax auditors later determine was an inter-state supply requiring IGST? Under Section 77 of the CGST Act read with Section 19 of the IGST Act: (1) The taxpayer MUST pay the correct IGST tax; and (2) The wrongly paid CGST+SGST will be refunded by the government upon filing a refund application. Crucially, the statute protects taxpayers from double interest: no interest under Section 50 can be charged on the belatedly paid correct tax, provided the wrong tax had been timely remitted to the treasury.

In this first part, we construct an enterprise Inter-State vs Intra-State Jurisdictional Engine in Python. We compare Location of Supplier against statutory Place of Supply, assign the correct tax components (CGST+SGST vs IGST), evaluate Section 77 / Section 19 error remediation protocols, and compute state revenue apportionment metrics.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, Tuple

@dataclass
class SupplyJurisdiction:
    invoice_id: str
    supplier_state_code: str    # e.g., '29' (Karnataka)
    place_of_supply_code: str   # e.g., '27' (Maharashtra)
    taxable_amount: float
    gst_rate: float
    tax_originally_charged: str # 'CGST_SGST' or 'IGST'

class JurisdictionEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def determine_tax_nature(sj: SupplyJurisdiction) -> Dict:
        is_intra_state = sj.supplier_state_code == sj.place_of_supply_code
        
        if is_intra_state:
            correct_tax_type = 'CGST_SGST'
            cgst_rate = sj.gst_rate / 2.0
            sgst_rate = sj.gst_rate / 2.0
            cgst_amount = sj.taxable_amount * cgst_rate
            sgst_amount = sj.taxable_amount * sgst_rate
            igst_amount = 0.0
            statutory_basis = 'Section 8 IGST Act: Supplier location and POS are in the same State (Intra-State).'
        else:
            correct_tax_type = 'IGST'
            cgst_amount = 0.0
            sgst_amount = 0.0
            igst_amount = sj.taxable_amount * sj.gst_rate
            statutory_basis = 'Section 7 IGST Act: Supplier location and POS are in different States (Inter-State).'
            
        is_mismatched = sj.tax_originally_charged != correct_tax_type
        remediation = 'None required. Correct tax was levied.'
        if is_mismatched:
            remediation = (
                f'Sec 77 CGST / Sec 19 IGST Triggered: Pay {correct_tax_type} without interest under Sec 50. '
                f'File Form GST RFD-01 to claim refund of wrongly paid {sj.tax_originally_charged}.'
            )
            
        return {
            'invoice_id': sj.invoice_id,
            'supplier_state': sj.supplier_state_code,
            'place_of_supply': sj.place_of_supply_code,
            'is_intra_state': is_intra_state,
            'correct_tax_classification': correct_tax_type,
            'cgst_payable': round(cgst_amount, 2),
            'sgst_payable': round(sgst_amount, 2),
            'igst_payable': round(igst_amount, 2),
            'total_tax': round(cgst_amount + sgst_amount + igst_amount, 2),
            'tax_type_mismatch_detected': is_mismatched,
            'statutory_remediation_protocol': remediation,
            'legal_authority': statutory_basis
        }

tx1 = SupplyJurisdiction('INV-1001', '29', '27', 1000000.0, 0.18, 'CGST_SGST')
engine = JurisdictionEngine()
res = engine.determine_tax_nature(tx1)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Validates Section 7 & 8 IGST Act jurisdictional rules, automatically flagging wrongly charged tax and invoking Section 77 / Section 19 zero-interest remediation protocols.
parts.example: A Bengaluru supplier (State 29) delivers machinery to a Mumbai factory (State 27). The supplier mistakenly bills 9% CGST ($90,000) and 9% SGST ($90,000). Upon tax audit, this is identified as an Inter-State supply. Under Section 19 IGST Act, the firm must pay $180,000 IGST (no interest charged) and apply for a refund of the $180,000 CGST/SGST.
parts.tryIt: Set place_of_supply_code to '29' (Karnataka) and tax_originally_charged to 'CGST_SGST'. Verify that is_intra_state becomes True and tax_type_mismatch_detected is False.

check.question: Under Section 77 of the CGST Act and Section 19 of the IGST Act, what happens if a taxpayer pays CGST and SGST on a transaction subsequently held to be an inter-state supply?
options: The taxpayer must pay the correct IGST, receives a full refund of the CGST/SGST paid, and is exempt from paying statutory interest on the delayed IGST.
The wrongly paid CGST/SGST is permanently confiscated by the state as an administrative evasion penalty.
The taxpayer is automatically subjected to mandatory search and seizure proceedings under Section 132.
The transaction is converted into an exempt supply with zero credit allowable on either leg.
check.why: Section 77(2) CGST Act explicitly provides that a registered person who paid CGST/SGST on a supply subsequently held to be inter-state shall pay IGST, but shall not be liable to pay any interest on the amount of IGST so paid.

parts.title: Place of Supply for Goods: Section 10 Mechanics & The Bill-To Ship-To Architecture
parts.say:
Determining the Place of Supply for physical goods is governed by Section 10 of the IGST Act for domestic transactions (and Section 11 for cross-border imports and exports). Unlike services, physical goods have tangible spatial coordinates, but complex multi-party commercial trade patterns often decouple the billing entity from the physical delivery location.

Section 10(1) establishes five distinct statutory scenarios for domestic goods: (a) Movement of Goods: Where the supply involves movement of goods (by supplier, recipient, or common carrier), POS is the location of the goods at the time at which movement terminates for delivery to the recipient; (b) Bill-to Ship-to Tri-Party Transactions: Where goods are delivered by the supplier to a recipient on the instruction of a third person, it is legally deemed that the third person has received the goods, and the POS is the principal place of business of such third person; (c) No Movement: Where supply does not involve movement of goods (e.g., purchasing factory machinery in-situ), POS is the location of such goods at the time of delivery to the recipient; (d) Assembly or Installation: Where goods are assembled or installed at site (e.g., industrial elevators or wind turbines), POS is the place of such installation; and (e) On-Board a Conveyance: Where goods are supplied on board a passenger train, aircraft, or vessel, POS is the location where such goods are taken on board.

The 'Bill-to Ship-to' architecture under Section 10(1)(b) is the backbone of modern supply chains. Consider a tri-party transaction: Buyer B in Gujarat orders goods from Manufacturer A in Karnataka, instructing A to deliver them directly to Client C in Maharashtra. Section 10(1)(b) creates a legal fiction breaking this into two simultaneous supplies: Leg 1 (A to B): Supplier in Karnataka, POS in Gujarat (IGST charged by A to B); Leg 2 (B to C): Supplier in Gujarat, POS in Maharashtra (IGST charged by B to C). A transports the goods directly from Karnataka to Maharashtra, but tax credits flow smoothly across the corporate balance sheets without jurisdictional disruption.

In this second part, we program an enterprise Section 10 Place of Supply for Goods Engine in Python. We implement the complete decision tree across movement, assembly at site, and tri-party bill-to ship-to structures, generate dual-leg invoice data, and validate e-way bill consignment compliance.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, Optional

@dataclass
class GoodsTradePattern:
    trade_id: str
    pattern_type: str        # 'MOVEMENT', 'BILL_TO_SHIP_TO', 'ASSEMBLY_SITE', 'NO_MOVEMENT', 'ON_BOARD'
    supplier_state: str
    buyer_billing_state: str # Third person in Bill-to Ship-to
    actual_delivery_state: str
    assembly_installation_state: str
    onboard_loading_state: str
    goods_value: float
    gst_rate: float

class Section10Engine:
    @staticmethod
    def resolve_pos(trade: GoodsTradePattern) -> Dict:
        if trade.pattern_type == 'MOVEMENT':
            # Sec 10(1)(a): Where movement terminates for delivery
            pos = trade.actual_delivery_state
            rule = 'Sec 10(1)(a): Location of goods at termination of movement.'
            is_inter = trade.supplier_state != pos
            tax_type = 'IGST' if is_inter else 'CGST_SGST'
            legs = [{'leg': 'Single Leg', 'supplier': trade.supplier_state, 'pos': pos, 'tax': tax_type}]
            
        elif trade.pattern_type == 'BILL_TO_SHIP_TO':
            # Sec 10(1)(b): Tri-party deeming fiction
            # Leg 1: Supplier -> Buyer (POS = Buyer Principal Place of Business)
            pos_leg1 = trade.buyer_billing_state
            tax_leg1 = 'IGST' if trade.supplier_state != pos_leg1 else 'CGST_SGST'
            # Leg 2: Buyer -> Recipient (POS = Actual Delivery Location under Sec 10(1)(a))
            pos_leg2 = trade.actual_delivery_state
            tax_leg2 = 'IGST' if trade.buyer_billing_state != pos_leg2 else 'CGST_SGST'
            
            pos = f'Leg1: {pos_leg1}, Leg2: {pos_leg2}'
            rule = 'Sec 10(1)(b): Deemed supply to third-party buyer, followed by onward supply.'
            legs = [
                {'leg': 'Leg 1 (Supplier to Buyer)', 'supplier': trade.supplier_state, 'pos': pos_leg1, 'tax': tax_leg1},
                {'leg': 'Leg 2 (Buyer to End Consignee)', 'supplier': trade.buyer_billing_state, 'pos': pos_leg2, 'tax': tax_leg2}
            ]
            
        elif trade.pattern_type == 'ASSEMBLY_SITE':
            # Sec 10(1)(d): Where goods are assembled/installed
            pos = trade.assembly_installation_state
            rule = 'Sec 10(1)(d): Place of assembly or installation at site.'
            is_inter = trade.supplier_state != pos
            tax_type = 'IGST' if is_inter else 'CGST_SGST'
            legs = [{'leg': 'Single Leg', 'supplier': trade.supplier_state, 'pos': pos, 'tax': tax_type}]
            
        else:
            pos = trade.actual_delivery_state
            rule = 'Default Sec 10 rules'
            legs = []
            
        return {
            'trade_id': trade.trade_id,
            'pattern': trade.pattern_type,
            'resolved_place_of_supply': pos,
            'governing_rule': rule,
            'transaction_legs': legs
        }

trade_tri_party = GoodsTradePattern(
    trade_id='TRD-550', pattern_type='BILL_TO_SHIP_TO',
    supplier_state='29 (Karnataka)', buyer_billing_state='24 (Gujarat)',
    actual_delivery_state='27 (Maharashtra)', assembly_installation_state='',
    onboard_loading_state='', goods_value=2000000.0, gst_rate=0.18
)
engine = Section10Engine()
res = engine.resolve_pos(trade_tri_party)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))

parts.example: An engineering firm in Delhi (State 07) contracts with a wind turbine manufacturer in Tamil Nadu (State 33) to assemble turbines at a wind farm in Rajasthan (State 08). Under Section 10(1)(d), the Place of Supply is Rajasthan (site of installation), making this an Inter-State supply subject to IGST.

check.question: Under Section 10(1)(b) of the IGST Act (Bill-to Ship-to model), what is the statutorily deemed Place of Supply for the transaction between the supplier and the third-party buyer?
options: The principal place of business of such third-party buyer on whose instruction goods are delivered.
The factory premises where the supplier originally manufactured the goods.
The physical destination warehouse of the ultimate consignee who unloads the truck.
The border checkpoint where the transport vehicle crossed state jurisdictional boundaries.
check.why: Section 10(1)(b) creates a statutory fiction that the goods are deemed to be received by the third person; hence, the Place of Supply is the principal place of business of that third person.

parts.title: Place of Supply for Domestic Services: Section 12 B2B vs B2C Jurisdictional Framework
parts.say:
Unlike physical goods, commercial services are intangible; a software developer in Hyderabad can debug an application running on cloud servers in Virginia while consulting with marketing executives in London. Because services lack physical weight and dimensions, the legislature created an intricate jurisdictional architecture under Section 12 of the IGST Act to determine the Place of Supply for domestic service transactions where both the supplier and recipient are located within India.

Section 12 operates through a fundamental dual-layer architecture: a 'General Default Rule' under Section 12(2), overlaid by twelve specific carve-out rules for specialized services (Section 12(3) to 12(14)). Under the General Default Rule of Section 12(2): (a) In a B2B transaction (supply made to a registered person), POS is the location of such registered recipient; (b) In a B2C transaction (supply made to an unregistered person), POS is the location of the recipient where the address on record exists, or the location of the supplier in all other cases.

However, the specialized carve-outs completely override the general rule: (1) Immovable Property Services under Section 12(3) (architects, civil engineers, hotel lodging, interior decorators): POS is the location where the immovable property is located or intended to be located. If an executive from a Mumbai company stays at a luxury hotel in Bengaluru, the POS is Karnataka; the hotel MUST charge CGST+SGST of Karnataka, which the Mumbai company cannot claim as ITC! (2) Performance-Based Personal Services under Section 12(4) (restaurant catering, personal grooming, fitness, beauty): POS is the location where services are actually performed; (3) Event Admission under Section 12(6): POS is the place where the event is held; (4) Transportation of Goods under Section 12(8): For B2B, location of registered recipient; for B2C, location where goods are handed over for transportation.

In this third part, we build an enterprise Section 12 Domestic Services POS Engine in Python. We ingest service engagement metadata, distinguish general B2B corporate retainers from immovable property and personal catering carve-outs, identify cross-state CGST/SGST credit trapping risks, and generate optimized corporate procurement guidelines.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict

@dataclass
class DomesticServiceSupply:
    engagement_id: str
    supplier_state: str
    service_category: str       # 'GENERAL_B2B_CONSULTING', 'HOTEL_ACCOMMODATION', 'RESTAURANT_DINING', 'EVENT_ORGANIZATION'
    is_recipient_registered_b2b: bool
    recipient_registered_state: str
    recipient_address_on_record_state: str
    immovable_property_state: str
    actual_performance_state: str
    fee_amount: float
    gst_rate: float

class Section12Engine:
    @staticmethod
    def resolve_service_pos(s: DomesticServiceSupply) -> Dict:
        pos = ''
        rule = ''
        itc_trapping_risk = False
        
        if s.service_category == 'HOTEL_ACCOMMODATION':
            # Sec 12(3)(b): Location where immovable property/hotel is located
            pos = s.immovable_property_state
            rule = 'Sec 12(3)(b): Immovable Property Location (Hotel site).'
            # Trapping risk: If buyer is in another state, local CGST+SGST cannot be claimed!
            if s.is_recipient_registered_b2b and s.recipient_registered_state != pos:
                itc_trapping_risk = True
                
        elif s.service_category == 'RESTAURANT_DINING':
            # Sec 12(4): Location where services are actually performed
            pos = s.actual_performance_state
            rule = 'Sec 12(4): Place of actual physical performance.'
            itc_trapping_risk = True  # Blocked under Sec 17(5) anyway
            
        elif s.service_category == 'GENERAL_B2B_CONSULTING':
            if s.is_recipient_registered_b2b:
                # Sec 12(2)(a): General B2B -> Location of registered recipient
                pos = s.recipient_registered_state
                rule = 'Sec 12(2)(a): General B2B default -> Location of registered recipient.'
            else:
                # Sec 12(2)(b): General B2C -> Address on record or supplier state
                pos = s.recipient_address_on_record_state or s.supplier_state
                rule = 'Sec 12(2)(b): General B2C default -> Address on record.'
                
        is_inter_state = s.supplier_state != pos
        tax_type = 'IGST' if is_inter_state else 'CGST_SGST'
        tax_val = s.fee_amount * s.gst_rate
        
        return {
            'engagement_id': s.engagement_id,
            'service_type': s.service_category,
            'supplier_state': s.supplier_state,
            'resolved_place_of_supply': pos,
            'statutory_authority': rule,
            'tax_classification': tax_type,
            'tax_amount': round(tax_val, 2),
            'itc_cross_state_trapping_risk': itc_trapping_risk
        }

# Test Hotel in Goa booked by Mumbai corporation
hotel = DomesticServiceSupply(
    engagement_id='SRV-880', supplier_state='30 (Goa)', service_category='HOTEL_ACCOMMODATION',
    is_recipient_registered_b2b=True, recipient_registered_state='27 (Maharashtra)',
    recipient_address_on_record_state='27 (Maharashtra)', immovable_property_state='30 (Goa)',
    actual_performance_state='30 (Goa)', fee_amount=250000.0, gst_rate=0.18
)
engine = Section12Engine()
res = engine.resolve_service_pos(hotel)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Implements Section 12 IGST Act rules for services, highlighting the cross-state credit trapping risk when out-of-state entities procure hotel accommodation.
parts.example: A software company in Maharashtra books an executive retreat at a luxury resort in Goa. Under Section 12(3), the Place of Supply is Goa. The resort charges Goa CGST+SGST. Because the company has no GST registration in Goa, it cannot claim the Goa CGST/SGST as ITC in its Maharashtra return, turning the tax into deadweight cost.
parts.tryIt: Change service_category to 'GENERAL_B2B_CONSULTING' and observe that POS shifts to Maharashtra under Sec 12(2)(a), making it an Inter-State supply with 100% claimable IGST.

check.question: Under Section 12(3)(b) of the IGST Act, what is the Place of Supply for lodging accommodation by a hotel or guest house?
options: The location where the hotel or immovable property is physically situated.
The principal registered business address of the corporate guest booking the room.
The state in which the online travel aggregator processing the payment has its headquarters.
The location where the corporate guest arrives at their home airport following the trip.
check.why: Section 12(3)(b) explicitly provides that the Place of Supply for services by way of lodging accommodation by a hotel, inn, or guest house shall be the location at which the immovable property is located.

parts.title: Cross-Border Services & Intermediaries: Section 13 Controversy & OIDAR Mechanics
parts.say:
When commercial transactions expand across national frontiers—where either the supplier or the recipient is located outside India—the domestic rules of Section 12 cease to apply. Instead, the transaction enters the jurisdiction of Section 13 of the IGST Act. Cross-border service taxation involves massive economic stakes: determining whether an engagement is a zero-rated export of services that brings tax-free foreign currency, or whether it constitutes an import of service subject to mandatory Reverse Charge under Section 9(3).

Under Section 13(2), the General Default Rule for cross-border services is that the Place of Supply is the 'Location of the Recipient of Services'. However, if the location of the recipient is not available in the ordinary course of business, the POS reverts to the location of the supplier. Overlaying this general rule are specialized international exceptions: (1) Performance-based services on physical goods under Section 13(3)(a): POS is where the services are physically performed (with an exception for job work on goods temporarily imported for repairs and re-exported); (2) Immovable property services under Section 13(4): POS is where the property is located; and (3) The notorious Section 13(8)(b) Intermediary Services rule.

Section 13(8)(b) has been one of the most contentious provisions in global tax law. Under Section 2(13), an 'Intermediary' is a broker, agent, or any other person who arranges or facilitates the supply of goods or services between two or more persons. Section 13(8)(b) dictates that for intermediary services, the Place of Supply is the 'Location of the Supplier'! Consequently, when an Indian entity facilitates global sales for an overseas US principal, the POS is deemed to be in India; the transaction FAILS to qualify as an export of service and is hit with 18% domestic GST! Finally, Section 13(12) governs Online Information Database Access and Retrieval (OIDAR) services (cloud streaming, SaaS, digital gaming): when supplied by overseas entities to non-taxable online recipients in India, POS is India, forcing foreign tech giants to register and remit GST.

In this fourth part, we engineer an enterprise Section 13 Cross-Border POS & OIDAR Engine in Python. We analyze master service agreements against the statutory intermediary definition, distinguish back-office processing (principal-to-principal) from sales facilitation (intermediary), evaluate OIDAR digital IP attributes, and determine export versus domestic tax exposure.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict

@dataclass
class CrossBorderService:
    engagement_id: str
    supplier_location: str       # 'INDIA' or 'OVERSEAS'
    recipient_location: str      # 'OVERSEAS' or 'INDIA'
    is_arranging_supply_for_others: bool # Intermediary test
    is_oidar_digital_service: bool       # Netflix, AWS SaaS, Steam
    is_recipient_registered_taxable: bool
    fee_in_foreign_currency_usd: float
    exchange_rate_inr: float

class Section13Engine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_cross_border(s: CrossBorderService) -> Dict:
        value_inr = s.fee_in_foreign_currency_usd * s.exchange_rate_inr
        
        if s.supplier_location == 'INDIA' and s.recipient_location == 'OVERSEAS':
            # Outbound Service from India
            if s.is_arranging_supply_for_others:
                # Sec 13(8)(b): Intermediary -> POS is Location of Supplier (INDIA)!
                pos = 'INDIA (Location of Supplier)'
                is_export = False
                gst_applicable = True
                reason = 'Sec 13(8)(b): Intermediary service. POS is supplier location (India). Disqualified from Export status!'
            else:
                # Sec 13(2): General Rule -> Location of Recipient (OVERSEAS)
                pos = 'OVERSEAS (Location of Recipient)'
                is_export = True
                gst_applicable = False  # Zero-rated under LUT
                reason = 'Sec 13(2): Principal-to-Principal IT/BPO service. POS overseas. Qualifies as Export.'
                
        elif s.supplier_location == 'OVERSEAS' and s.recipient_location == 'INDIA':
            # Inbound Service to India
            if s.is_oidar_digital_service:
                pos = 'INDIA (Sec 13(12) OIDAR)'
                is_export = False
                gst_applicable = True
                reason = 'Sec 13(12): OIDAR service to India. Overseas supplier must register under simplified GST scheme.'
            elif s.is_recipient_registered_taxable:
                pos = 'INDIA (Sec 13(2))'
                is_export = False
                gst_applicable = True
                reason = 'Import of Service by Indian Business. Taxable under Reverse Charge Mechanism (Sec 9(3)).'
            else:
                pos = 'OVERSEAS'
                is_export = False
                gst_applicable = False
                reason = 'Non-taxable import.'
                
        return {
            'engagement_id': s.engagement_id,
            'transaction_flow': f'{s.supplier_location} -> {s.recipient_location}',
            'resolved_pos': pos,
            'is_zero_rated_export': is_export,
            'is_gst_taxable': gst_applicable,
            'taxable_base_inr': round(value_inr, 2),
            'gst_liability_18pct': round(value_inr * 0.18, 2) if gst_applicable else 0.0,
            'legal_statutory_basis': reason
        }

# Case A: Pure IT Software Export vs Case B: Intermediary Sales Agent
it_export = CrossBorderService('ENG-EXP-01', 'INDIA', 'OVERSEAS', False, False, True, 100000.0, 83.5)
sales_agent = CrossBorderService('ENG-AGT-02', 'INDIA', 'OVERSEAS', True, False, True, 50000.0, 83.5)
engine = Section13Engine()
print('--- Pure IT Software Export ---')
print(json.dumps(engine.evaluate_cross_border(it_export), indent=2))
print('--- Intermediary Sales Agency ---')
print(json.dumps(engine.evaluate_cross_border(sales_agent), indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Simulates Section 13 IGST Act cross-border rules, demonstrating how the Section 13(8)(b) intermediary provision traps sales facilitation commissions in domestic GST.
parts.example: An Indian company provides outsourced software coding directly to a US enterprise for $500,000. POS is US under Section 13(2) (Zero-rated export, $0 GST). But an Indian marketing agency that connects US software sellers with Indian corporate buyers for a $50,000 commission is an Intermediary under Section 13(8)(b): POS is India, and 18% GST ($9,000) must be paid.
parts.tryIt: Set is_arranging_supply_for_others to False for the sales agency to demonstrate how restructuring into an independent market research contract restores export status.

check.question: Under Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act, what is the Place of Supply for an Intermediary service provided by an Indian entity to an overseas client?
options: The location of the supplier of services (India), thereby disqualifying the transaction from being an export of services.
The location of the overseas recipient, qualifying the transaction as a zero-rated export.
The sovereign territory where the underlying commercial goods are physically manufactured.
A split jurisdiction: 50% taxed in India and 50% taxed in the recipient's foreign nation.
check.why: Section 13(8)(b) explicitly dictates that the Place of Supply for intermediary services shall be the location of the supplier of services (India).

parts.title: Zero-Rated Supplies & SEZ Operations: Section 16 IGST Act & LUT Execution Protocols
parts.say:
To maintain national competitiveness in international trade, modern taxation frameworks operate under a universal economic tenet: 'Goods and services must be exported free of domestic taxes, but domestic taxes must not be exported.' In GST jurisprudence, this doctrine is codified under Section 16 of the IGST Act under the legal designation of 'Zero-Rated Supplies'. Zero-rating is not mere tax exemption: while an 'exempt supply' blocks Input Tax Credit under Section 17(2), a 'zero-rated supply' preserves 100% of input tax credits, allowing exporters to claim full cash refunds of all input taxes embedded in their supply chain.

Under Section 16(1), zero-rated supplies comprise two exclusive categories: (a) Export of goods or services; and (b) Supply of goods or services to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) developer or an SEZ unit. To qualify as an 'Export of Services' under Section 2(6) of the IGST Act, five cumulative statutory conditions must be simultaneously proven: (1) The supplier of service is located in India; (2) The recipient of service is located outside India; (3) The Place of Supply of service is outside India (under Section 13); (4) Payment for such service has been received in convertible foreign exchange (or in Indian Rupees wherever permitted by the Reserve Bank of India); and (5) The supplier and recipient are NOT merely establishments of a distinct person in accordance with Explanation 1 in Section 8.

Under Section 16(3) and 16(4), an exporter can execute zero-rated supplies through two distinct statutory routes: (Route 1) Supply under a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) or Bond without payment of IGST, and subsequently claim a cash refund of unutilized accumulated Input Tax Credit under Section 54(3); or (Route 2) Supply with payment of IGST and claim an automated refund of the IGST paid. Most enterprises opt for the LUT route via Form GST RFD-11, preserving working capital by completely bypassing the cash payment of export taxes.

In this fifth part, we build an enterprise Section 16 Zero-Rated Export & LUT Compliance Engine in Python. We audit transactions against the 5 cumulative statutory tests of Section 2(6), manage annual LUT Form GST RFD-11 validation, compute refund entitlements under the Formula in Rule 89(4), and track realization timelines within the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) 9-month statutory window.

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List

@dataclass
class ExportAuditCandidate:
    export_id: str
    is_supplier_in_india: bool
    is_recipient_outside_india: bool
    is_pos_outside_india: bool
    received_in_convertible_forex: bool
    is_separate_legal_entity: bool # Not merely distinct branch
    has_valid_lut_rfd11: bool
    turnover_zero_rated_export: float
    total_turnover: float
    net_itc_pool_inputs_services: float

class Section16ExportEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def audit_export_of_services(cand: ExportAuditCandidate) -> Dict:
        # Test 5 cumulative conditions of Section 2(6) IGST Act
        c1 = cand.is_supplier_in_india
        c2 = cand.is_recipient_outside_india
        c3 = cand.is_pos_outside_india
        c4 = cand.received_in_convertible_forex
        c5 = cand.is_separate_legal_entity
        
        qualifies_as_export = c1 and c2 and c3 and c4 and c5
        
        if not qualifies_as_export:
            failed = []
            if not c1: failed.append('Supplier not in India')
            if not c2: failed.append('Recipient not outside India')
            if not c3: failed.append('Place of Supply is within India')
            if not c4: failed.append('Forex remittance not received')
            if not c5: failed.append('Merely distinct branch establishments')
            return {
                'export_id': cand.export_id,
                'qualifies_as_zero_rated_export': False,
                'disqualification_reasons': failed,
                'refundable_itc_under_rule89_4': 0.0
            }
            
        # If qualified under LUT:
        # Rule 89(4) Formula: Refund = (Turnover of Zero Rated / Adjusted Total Turnover) * Net ITC
        turnover_ratio = cand.turnover_zero_rated_export / cand.total_turnover if cand.total_turnover > 0 else 0.0
        maximum_refundable_itc = turnover_ratio * cand.net_itc_pool_inputs_services
        
        return {
            'export_id': cand.export_id,
            'qualifies_as_zero_rated_export': True,
            'statutory_compliance': 'All 5 cumulative conditions under Sec 2(6) IGST Act fulfilled.',
            'lut_protection_active': cand.has_valid_lut_rfd11,
            'export_turnover_ratio': round(turnover_ratio * 100.0, 2),
            'net_itc_pool_available': cand.net_itc_pool_inputs_services,
            'rule89_4_cash_refund_entitlement': round(maximum_refundable_itc, 2),
            'recommended_compliance_action': 'File Form GST RFD-01 under Category: Refund of unutilized ITC on zero-rated supplies.'
        }

exp1 = ExportAuditCandidate(
    export_id='EXP-SaaS-901', is_supplier_in_india=True, is_recipient_outside_india=True,
    is_pos_outside_india=True, received_in_convertible_forex=True,
    is_separate_legal_entity=True, has_valid_lut_rfd11=True,
    turnover_zero_rated_export=8000000.0, total_turnover=10000000.0,
    net_itc_pool_inputs_services=900000.0
)
engine = Section16ExportEngine()
res = engine.audit_export_of_services(exp1)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))

It accumulates $900,000 in unutilized ITC on cloud server infrastructure and rent. Under Section 16(3) read with Rule 89(4), the company receives a cash bank refund of 80% * $900,000 = $720,000 directly from the tax treasury.

check.question: Under Section 2(6) of the IGST Act, which of the following is NOT one of the 5 mandatory conditions to qualify as an 'Export of Services'?
options: The transaction must be physically inspected and sealed by an officer of Customs at an international port of exit.
The payment for such service must be received in convertible foreign exchange (or permissible INR).
The Place of Supply of the service must be outside India.
The supplier of service and the recipient of service must not merely be establishments of a distinct person.
check.why: Customs physical inspection applies to goods, not intangible services. The 5 conditions for services are: supplier in India, recipient outside India, POS outside India, convertible forex received, and not merely distinct branch establishments.
